articles.title: Victoria Beckham, ‘duck face’ and onesies: nine things Zoolander predicted about fashion
articles.summary: It’s been 25 years since the release of this film skewering an industry that famously takes itself very seriously. It might have been comedy gold but it was also, in its own way, prophetic. • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here.
body: Critics were divided, the US release date couldn’t have been worse (a few days after 9/11) and the sequel was a flop. Yet few films have predicted fashion’s own present like 2001’s Zoolander. The memeable absurdist comedy about the “three-times male model of the year” was a cinematic Cassandra: correctly predicting themes, styles and sensibilities of the industry that still ring true today.

The joke around Derek Zoolander’s trademark look, the Blue Steel, was how ridiculous it was. Still, the shocked but vacant stare with the exaggerated pout later became the facial pose on social media. Officially defined as “duck face” (after the Japanese term “ahiru-guchi”, duck mouth), the look gained traction on Instagram in the early 2010s, when people finally took a break from smizing. But tweakments such as lip-filler and forehead botox mean that faces have begun artificially morphing into the pose. So now everyone can be really, really, really Zoolander, without even trying.

articles.title: Make Me Well by Xand van Tulleken – an eye-opening takedown of wellness myths
articles.summary: The engaging TV doctor dismantles the spurious science behind modern day snake oils, from collagen to turmeric. When Xand van Tulleken set off on a journey into the wild west of wellness, he didn’t expect to discover anything new about vitamin D.
body: The tiggerish TV doctor and twin brother to Chris (he’s the one who wrote Ultra-Processed People about the food industry) qualified at a time of high excitement in vitamin D circles; in the early 2000s, big studies were linking it not just to bone health but cancer, heart disease and dementia. “The range of potential problems to be solved was dizzying,” Van Tulleken writes in Make Me Well.

But – spoiler alert – it turns out evidence even of the benefits of the most medically endorsed supplement shrivels under scrutiny. After immersing himself in decades of trials and speaking to a professor who had devoted his career to what he now views as the false promise of vitamin D, Van Tulleken finds no justification for its routine consumption for all but a tiny proportion of the population who are genuinely deficient.

articles.title: The Scoop With Completedworks’s Anna Jewsbury: On The Brand’s New London Store
articles.summary: This week’s guest is Anna Jewsbury, who founded London design brand Completedworks with her brother Mark in 2013. Completedworks hit the mainstream during the pandemic, when cool-girl celebrities began appearing in fashion magazine roundups wearing the brand’s scrunchie earrings.
body: Welcome to The Scoop, a weekly email series in which I ask fashion insiders to give me a piece of news they haven’t shared elsewhere.

But it was a few years later when Completedworks really broke through the noise: in February 2024, the brand staged a surprise performance by actress Joanna Lumley to present its FW24 collection. On a stage covered in scattered magazines and pieces of burnt toast, Lumley enacted a monologue by novelist Fatima Farheen Mirza about the mundanity of life. It was a brilliant piece of marketing because it went a little beyond marketing — the pieces of jewelry became part of the set, even though they were really the reason we were all there in the first place.

Dianna Agron, Debi Mazar and Jemima Kirke starred in subsequent seasons, making Completedworks one of London Fashion Week’s hottest tickets. My son even asked if we were going to see “the lady who got sad” again this London Fashion Week. So this September, when there was no show… I called Anna to find out why.

articles.title: Experience: I rate benches
articles.summary: My Instagram page started as something to amuse my friends, but it took off – and led to me meeting Sophie, who is now my wife. The idea came to me in summer 2019, when I finished studying at Swansea University. One day I went walking with friends around the beautiful Penllergare Valley woods.
body: I noticed that someone had left flowers on the bench. I wondered who had put them there, who they were for, and why they’d chosen this location. By the time we reached the next bench along the route, I was deep in thought about all the people who had sat there before me.

Both benches had beautiful views, and my friends and I started comparing them. I joked that someone should start rating benches of the world. In the following days, I set up an Instagram account called RateThisBench and then posted a handful of reviews of benches near my family home in Bristol, mostly to amuse my friends.
At the end of the summer, I planned to close the account. But my dad, Chris, had become quite invested in it. It became our joint project; after dinner we’d go out for a walk and assess a bench.
I wasn’t interested in growing the account, but the page took off. I suddenly had hundreds of followers – I’m currently at about 27,500.

articles.title: Helen Goh’s recipe for baked oats with morello cherries and almond | The sweet spot
articles.summary: This moreish, flapjack-style oaty bake, flavoured with maple syrup and dotted with sour cherries, works as well for dessert as it does for breakfast. I’ve been making versions of these baked oats ever since discovering Heidi Swanson’s recipe in Super Natural Every Day.
body: Jarred cherries come in many forms, so if yours is more like a compote or jam, simply add it in small teaspoonfuls instead.
Heat the oven to 195C (175C fan)/385F/gas 5½ and lightly grease a 26cm ovenproof dish that’s about 5-6cm deep – the oat mixture will form a fairly shallow layer.

Put the oats, baking powder, cinnamon and salt in a medium bowl, mix well, then tip into the greased dish. In a large jug, whisk the egg, maple syrup and melted butter, then add the coconut drinking milk and vanilla, and whisk again to combine. Pour this evenly over the oats, then gently press down any oats that remain dry.

Dot the drained cherries evenly over the oats. If using a thicker compote or jam, drop small teaspoonfuls over the surface, then use the tip of the spoon to drag each one out slightly, creating ripples rather than deep pools. Scatter over the flaked almonds.
points: This moreish, flapjack-style oaty bake, flavoured with maple syrup and dotted with sour cherries, works as well for dessert as it does for breakfast.

articles.title: Exclusive: Inside the After-Party for Kate Berlant’s New Special, ‘Parmesan’
articles.summary: The actor and comedian toasted the release of her new HBO special, “Parmesan,” with an after-party for the ages.
body: Berlant’s new hour-long HBO special, Parmesan —out October 16—is as delightfully embodied as ever—but it also sees her tread some sensitive new territory. Berlant doesn’t refer to her current partner, musician Naomi McPherson, by name, but she does touch on her queer awakening as a 30-something, mentioning her “lesbian boyfriend” in the waiting room while Berlant froze her eggs.

Yet McPherson—who is credited as an executive producer on the special—was happily on hand to support Berlant at both an early screening of Parmesan at Brain Dead Studios in Los Angeles on Wednesday and the after-party at legendary drag bar Plaza Nightclub.

“I was exceptionally nervous, in a way that I was not expecting, to watch the special with my friends and people that I respect so much,” Berlant told me in a room stuffed with dragtastic feathered headpieces and jewel-toned gowns at Plaza, clad in Bottega Veneta herself. “Stand-up is an inherently embarrassing art form, and there’s nowhere to hide. I felt a little out-of-body watching it.”
points: The actor and comedian toasted the release of her new HBO special, “Parmesan,” with an after-party for the ages.

articles.title: In Morocco's High Atlas Mountains, Joining One of the Oldest Migrations in Africa
articles.summary: Writer Jen Murphy joins a nomadic Berber family as they bring the herds from their high altitude grazing grounds to the edge of the Sahara—and finds a profound beauty in the land and its keepers.
body: A persistent chorus of shrill bleats and guttural baas echo across the canyons and basalt towers of Jebel Saghro. I squint against the midday sun. In the distance, high on a rocky peak, I spot the red djellaba worn by Telhou Belâawane, the matriarch of the Berber family I am traveling with in Morocco. Her presence confirms that the goats are near. I squint again, searching the crags and stony folds of the mountains for our herd. But to my untrained eye, their onyx-coats are frustratingly indistinguishable from the volcanic terrain.

Jebel Saghro is the ancestral homeland of Telhou’s people, the Aït Atta, a historically powerful Berber (or Amazigh, which means free people) tribe in southeast Morocco. This rugged region unfurls from the High Atlas Mountains to the edge of the Sahara and twice each year it serves as the backdrop for one of the oldest migrations in Africa. For millennia, Aït Atta and other Berber families have moved their livestock upwards of 180 miles from the summer grazing grounds of the High Atlas to the winter pastures of Jebel Saghro. This seasonal pastoral journey, known as transhumance, defines a semi-nomadic way of life that is rapidly disappearing.
points: Writer Jen Murphy joins a nomadic Berber family as they bring the herds from their high altitude grazing grounds to the edge of the Sahara—and finds a profound beauty in the land and its keepers.

articles.title: These Resorts Offer a Real Taste of American Regional Cuisine
articles.summary: American resorts are once again having a moment — and it’s not pickleball partisans driving the trend. A new generation of travelers, beset with decision fatigue in their daily lives, are embracing the all-inclusive stay where activities, amenities, and dining are all on the menu and usually just a…
body: Fortunately, stress-free no longer needs to mean bland or generic when it comes to cuisine and culture. Resorts have begun forging deep culinary connections to their surroundings, far beyond merely offering a few regionally specific cocktails or themed burger toppings.

Onsite farms, creameries, and distilleries provide fresh ingredients with true terroir, as well as a new category of resort activity: food-and-drink-focused tours and workshops to fill the time between morning yoga and an afternoon poolside nap.

Some resort restaurants, like Clay at Wildflower Farms in New York’s Hudson Valley and Sierra Mar at the Post Ranch Inn in Big Sur, California, have become destinations in themselves, where star chefs take diners deep into a region’s foodways.
These resorts leave visitors not just relaxed but also satisfied, having truly experienced — and tasted — a particular place.

articles.title: Enjoy Fishing, Foraging, and Focaccia-Making at These U.S. Resorts
articles.summary: Plenty of resorts across the country have excellent restaurants, but travelers seeking more should explore the hands-on side of culinary resort experiences. From New York’s Hudson Valley to the South Texas Coast, adventurous food lovers can partake in workshops and experiences that get them out of…
body: Guests today expect more than a Michelin-starred restaurant. They want to get into the kitchen and out in the field.

At these properties, it’s less about what’s on your plate and more about how it got there. Big Sur is the perfect place to forage for edible botanicals and aromatics, and on Chesapeake Bay, harvesting and shucking oysters is woven into the community’s cultural fabric. Those wanting to escape the hustle and bustle of New York City can head up to the Hudson Valley for focaccia-making, while a desert oasis on the outskirts of Scottsdale, Arizona, teaches you how to craft pasta like a pro.

No matter your level of expertise, these resort experiences are designed to connect curious travelers with an impressive network of chefs, farmers, ecologists, mixologists, and bakers. For a vacation that will also quench your thirst for knowledge, head to these exciting culinary resorts.
